subtitle: How NASA Ames implemented an ARPANET file transfer server on IBM TSS/360, with comments on the protocol.

tldr.problem: The ARPANET file transfer protocol had to be mapped onto the dataset and catalog conventions of IBM's TSS/360 system.
tldr.mechanism: The server maps TSS catalogs and record-structured datasets onto the transfer commands, using stream or record conventions for structured and unstructured data.
tldr.outcome: The note also comments on the current protocol (RFC 354) and offers suggestions for future enhancements. The scan is poorly legible, so only its readable parts are summarized.

today: RFC 418 has status Unknown in the metadata and no recorded replacement. It records one early ARPANET file transfer server implementation.

sections.title: Purpose
sections.content:
RFC 418, dated November 27, 1972, describes the initial implementation of Server File Transfer at the NASA Ames Research Center. It also contains comments on the current file transfer protocol (RFC 354 and a companion RFC) and some suggestions for future enhancements.

The scanned text is only partly legible, so this summary covers just the parts that can be read. See RFC 354 for the protocol itself.
sections.eli5: A report on how one big computer was taught to share files over the network.

sections.title: TSS Files and Catalogs
sections.content:
Each user of TSS is assigned a user identification (USERID), normally formed from a three letter organization code and the user's initials. Each userid has its own catalog holding pointers to all datasets, whose names are made up of one or more parts of up to eight characters separated by periods.

Datasets can be shared among users by permitting and then explicitly sharing them. A shared entry points to the owner's catalog entry, so the owner can change or remove sharing at any time. Only disk datasets in the virtual access method (VAM) are supported by the server.
sections.eli5: Every user has a personal list of files, and files can be shared by pointing to the owner's entry.

sections.title: Structured and Unstructured Data
sections.content:
All TSS files have some record structure, and a record may be up to one million bytes long. The server sends structured data (STRU R) with an end-of-record sequence added to each record, and unstructured data (STRU F) with none added.

When receiving structured data, an end-of-record sequence is required to define each TSS record, with a maximum record length of 1012 bytes. Unstructured data is written into arbitrary sized records. The goal is that any file sent to TSS can be retrieved exactly as sent.
sections.eli5: Some files are lines of text and some are just a stream of bits, so the server treats them differently when saving.

sections.title: Server Commands
sections.content:
The maximum length of a command and its parameters is 256 characters. Blanks are removed, so they matter only to separate a command from its parameters. Only one command may be used with no active user logged on; all others require a prior USER command.

USER sets the TSS userid used for catalog access and resets transfer parameters to defaults. File transfer passwords are optional, and the demonstration userids ARPA, ARPA1 and ARPA2 have none. The ACCT command is not supported.
sections.eli5: You must say who you are first, and then you can ask for files.

references.text: RFC 354, the file transfer protocol discussed in the note.
